/* styles/base.css — palette, reset, typography (GDD §7, sprite style guide) */

:root {
  --bg: #0d0b08;
  --bg-raise: #171310;
  --panel: #241d15;
  --line: #3a3226;
  --line-soft: #4a4034;
  /* Map STRUCTURE — the roads and plain rings a player reads to plan a run
     (#45, Sunna's ruling: 3:1 on each glyph's identifying boundary against each
     adjacent rendered colour). --line-soft's atmospheric value measures 1.93
     (edge vs field) / 1.72 (ring vs its own fill) from rendered pixels — below
     every defensible floor — but its 27 other consumers are text-adjacent soft
     lines that keep the atmospheric look ("atmospheric elsewhere"). So the map
     graph rides its own token: #7a6b54 clears both adjacencies with margin
     (rendered 3.78 vs field, 3.36 worst adjacency) while staying the visibly
     dimmer sibling of high contrast's 4.19 — two settings, two looks.
     Evidence: tools/contrast-audit.mjs --profile hi-contrast-off;
     the former atmospheric map-structure proposal (R2; removed 2026-10-11, see git history). */
  --map-structure: #7a6b54;
  --parchment: #e8dcc0;
  --muted: #8e826a;
  --gold: #c9a227;
  --accent-rgb: 201, 162, 39; /* --gold as rgb, for glow/halo alpha (swapped by accent theme) */
  --blood: #8a1a1a;
  /* The HP resource fill — the approved hybrid's owner pixel (2026-08-13,
     claude-family falk-family hybrid-confirmation, F1-resource-health.png),
     minted as its OWN token so the accent themes keep owning the palette
     (cb-safe swaps it below). Before this token the hp row wore var(--blood)
     and the conflict was recorded, not resolved: token vs owner hex. Now both
     hold — the value is the owner's, the swap is the theme's. --blood keeps
     its 16 other consumers (map rings, danger buttons, enemy hpbars) and is
     NOT this token. */
  --res-hp: #a43c35;
  --rot: #b5541c;
  --frost: #7fa8c9;
  --grace: #9fc3e8;
  --ember: #e46a44;
  --green: #7fd97f;
  /* THE KEYWORD TINT CARD TEXT USES, and it is a token because it is a fact
     about a WORD, not about a container. It had no token, so the one palette
     that wanted a different answer had nowhere to put it and put it in a
     SELECTOR instead (`body.cb-safe .card .ctext .st-bleed`, deleted below).
     When the five mark rules re-keyed `.card .ctext` → `.ctext` so the Smith
     preview could wear them too, every token-based rule came through for free
     and that one hardcoded hex stayed behind on the old container — so under
     Colorblind-friendly the SAME WORD read reddish-purple on a card face and
     vermillion in the preview. The hex was the reason it could not follow.
     Derived from --ember, not restated: in the default palette Bleed wears the
     ember hue TODAY, and that is a derivation, not a copy — one home for the
     value. Colorblind-friendly overrides it once, below, which is the only
     place the two diverge.
     OPEN, AND FREJA'S, NOT MINE: whether the DEFAULT palette should diverge
     too. It does not today — a Bleed keyword and a number the upgrade made
     WORSE both render rgb(201,80,46) on every screen, one hue doing two jobs
     on one line. Colorblind-friendly already answers that question `yes`. */
  --bleed: var(--ember);
  /* THE TAP-TARGET FLOOR, and it has one home because it is one fact.
     Sunna's ruling under Law 4 (#37): "a floor of N device px measured after
     zoom; a floor is not a ceiling." The whole app is scaled by `zoom:
     var(--ui-zoom)` on <body>, so a length L below body renders at L x zoom
     device px — dividing by the zoom here is what makes N mean N ON GLASS
     rather than N in a coordinate space the finger has never heard of. It is
     the same conversion the rest of the app does through fx.js, expressed as a
     unit so a rule can just use it.
     px, DELIBERATELY, and this is exactly the case Law 2 admits: a finger does
     not get bigger when a player raises Text size. Law 4 is the other half of
     the same sentence — text scaling must stop scaling non-text UI — so a
     control that held text at 4.4rem was wrong in two directions at once.

     `--tap-target` IS THE CONSTANT, AND IT IS NOT WRITTEN HERE. It is the
     player's Minimum tap size (Settings → Accessibility, default 44), written
     onto <html> by applyTapSize() in src/main.js exactly where applyUiScale()
     already writes `--ui-zoom`. This calc keeps its shape; only the number
     moved out of it, to `balance.ui.tapSize` — the one place a number a player
     can tune is allowed to live (Law 1 clause 2).

     AND THERE IS NO `, 44px` FALLBACK IN THIS LINE, deliberately. A literal
     here would agree with balance.ui.tapSize.def today and be synchronised by
     nothing — the second copy this house exists to catch, planted in the very
     line whose job is to hold one home. If `--tap-target` is ever unwritten
     the floor vanishes and every floored control drops to 21–31 device px,
     which is loud on the screen and is what `node tools/tapsize.mjs` measures.
     A quietly-correct-looking 44 is the failure Law 0 clause 5 names; a
     missing floor is not quiet. */
  --tap-floor: calc(var(--tap-target) / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
  /* THE ICON-BUTTON HIT BOX. Close and ☰ reserve the same tap-safe square on
     every component. The close control paints a smaller face inside that box,
     but its pointer, touch, and focus target remains this shared length:
     a floor lets a tall row or a big title stretch the control, and then the
     shape a player learned on one door is a different shape on the next.
     Width AND height read this; nothing else sizes them. It is the tap floor
     by value, so it still clears the floor at every UI size and zoom. */
  --iconbtn-size: var(--tap-floor);
  /* THE FLOOR, FROZEN AT THE DEFAULT — for the one control that is exempt from
     the floor it sets. Marina's ruling: Minimum tap size is the only control in
     the game whose resizing happens WHILE IT IS BEING PRESSED, so its own four
     chips hold still at the default and everything else on the screen still
     resizes under the player's eye. Measured cause: at the 44 step the pressed
     chip landed 61.44 device px from the finger, because the whole group
     re-lays-out — wider than a fingertip, and no `scrollTop` answers a
     horizontal reflow.
     Same single datum: applyTapSize() writes `--tap-floor-default-target` from
     balance.ui.tapSize.def, the same `def` the row's own default reads — not a
     second copy of 44, the same 44 asked a second question. Divided by the zoom
     for the reason --tap-floor is: an exempt control a small phone shrinks
     anyway is an exemption in name only. */
  --tap-floor-default: calc(var(--tap-floor-default-target) / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
  /* THE CORNER SCALE, AND WHY IT IS A CLOSED SET.
     Measured 2026-09-02 by driving 78 surfaces (every ?shot= state, every
     settings category, the quick menu, all three Armoury views) at 1440x900 and
     390x844 and reading computed style off every rendered button: TWENTY
     distinct border-radius values on one control layer — 0, 1.8, 2, 3, 4, 5.83,
     6, 6.5, 7.78, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 14.44, 50%, 999px and a
     two-corner pair. A player cannot read twenty roundnesses as meaning
     anything, so they mean nothing, and every new rule had twenty precedents to
     copy. This is the set instead. Snapping is BOUNDED: no declaration moved
     more than 2px, which is why the sweep could be mechanical and reviewed as a
     diff rather than re-judged surface by surface.

     FOUR STEPS, NAMED BY WHAT WEARS THEM, not by size — a rule should be able to
     ask "what am I?" rather than "how round?":
       --r-1  tags, keycaps, inline pills — the small stuff inside a row
       --r-2  small controls — segmented chips, inputs, icon buttons
       --r-3  buttons, cards, list rows, tiles — the things a finger presses
       --r-4  panels and modal shells — the things that hold the above

     THE ROLES ARE READ OFF THE TREE, NOT IMPOSED ON IT. Every step is a value
     the app already used most often for that job, which is what let the sweep
     stay inside 2px; a scale that argued with the design would have cost a
     re-judgement of all 168 declarations instead of a diff.

     REM RADII WERE A BUG THIS SET RETIRES, and it is the same defect Law 4
     already names in the Text size block below: a radius written in rem grows
     when the player raises Text size, so the title modal's corners were a
     function of the font. Non-text geometry is px here for that reason.

     THE `-glass` VARIANTS ARE NOT A FIFTH STEP. `zoom: var(--ui-zoom)` on
     <body> scales every length below it, so a control that must hold the SAME
     roundness on the screen at every UI size divides by the zoom — the same
     conversion --tap-floor makes above, for the same reason. Combat's HUD
     already did this by hand in five places; these are those five, named.

     NOT IN THE SET, deliberately: `45% 45% 55% 55%` on the refusal blob, which
     is a drawn shape rather than a corner, and `border-radius: 0`, which is a
     rule saying "square on purpose" and stays legible as a literal. */
  --r-1: 3px;
  --r-2: 6px;
  --r-3: 8px;
  --r-4: 12px;
  --r-pill: 999px;
  --r-round: 50%;
  --r-1-glass: calc(var(--r-1) / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
  --r-2-glass: calc(var(--r-2) / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
  --r-3-glass: calc(var(--r-3) / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
  --r-4-glass: calc(var(--r-4) / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
  /* CONTROL TYPE — FOUR STEPS, AND AN HONEST BOUNDARY ON HOW FAR THEY REACH.
     The same census that found twenty corner values found TWENTY-ONE font
     size/family pairs on buttons: Cinzel at 5.8, 7, 9, 10, 10.5, 11.5, 12, 13,
     13.5, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 and 20px, and Inter at 9, 11, 12, 14 and 15 —
     across ONE control layer, with two typefaces sharing it. Some of those are
     one rule read at two UI zooms (16.67 and 20 are the title menu; 13.33 and
     13.5 are BACK/CONTINUE), which is honest scaling. The rest is drift.

     THESE FOUR ARE THE SCALE. `button` and `button.subtle` — the two rules every
     other control inherits from — now name a step instead of a number, and so
     do the modal action buttons, whose 1.35rem was an arbitrary point between
     two steps that already existed.

     WHAT IS NOT DONE, SAID HERE RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER: the ~40 component
     rules that override button type for their own geometry are UNSWEPT. A
     corner can be snapped mechanically because it changes nothing else; a font
     size reflows the box it is in, and those rules are entangled with grid
     templates and min-heights that were tuned around the current values. Each
     is a judgement against its own surface, not a find-and-replace, and doing
     them blind is how a type scale ships a regression. The scale is here so
     that work has somewhere to land. */
  --t-1: 1rem;
  --t-2: 1.2rem;
  --t-3: 1.5rem;
  --t-4: 1.8rem;
  --font-display: 'Cinzel', Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif;
  --font-body: Inter, 'Segoe UI', system-ui, sans-serif;
}

/* Root text anchor: 62.5% makes 1rem = 10px at Text M. The Text-size setting
   overrides this value for type and line metrics; component geometry must not
   derive from this calibration. */
html { height: var(--visible-height, 100dvh); overflow: hidden; font-size: 62.5%; }
/* AIM AT THE FAR ENEMY, LEAVE THE GAME — Sunna's gate finding on #22, measured
   both edges x3. The straight line from the leftmost card to the far-right
   enemy runs at 38 deg, under the ~45-47 deg boundary where Chromium claims a
   drag as horizontal scroll. The hand rests at scrollLeft 0, so the claimed
   scroll has nothing to move and CHAINS TO THE VIEWPORT — and Chrome's
   overscroll navigation goes BACK, out of combat, mid-fight. `pan-x` on the
   cards is what routes the shallow aim into the horizontal machinery: the
   known-bad survived the same swipe 3/3, the first cut of the fix survived 0/3.

   THE RULE MUST SIT AT THE ROOT AND SHE MEASURED WHY: `overscroll-behavior-x:
   contain` on .hand does NOT close it — at scrollLeft 0 the hand cannot scroll
   rightward, so it is never the scroll target; the viewport is. Here, it closes
   3/3 with hand scrolling intact (150->200).

   BOTH AXES, DELIBERATELY, and the halves have different evidence: -x is
   measured (her backnav.mjs, both edges). -y is the SAME mechanism pointed the
   other way — pull-to-refresh reloading a live run off any vertical overscroll —
   declared here because this app is a fullscreen game with overflow:hidden at
   the root and NO surface where a browser navigation or refresh gesture is ever
   the player's intent; there is nothing for `none` to take away. Headless
   Chromium cannot raise pull-to-refresh, so the -y half ships as a declaration
   with this named boundary, not as a measured green. */
html, body { overscroll-behavior: none; }
/* PROTOTYPE (EldenSpire#23, track B) — 100dvh, and ONLY here.
   `dvh` was pitched as a sweep. It is wrong everywhere except this one line,
   and the reason is the one that has bitten this file all week. Measured under
   `body { zoom: 0.62 }` at 390x844: 100dvh, 100svh, 100lvh AND 100vh all
   compute to 843.98px and then render at 523 visual — vh-family units resolve
   against the UNZOOMED viewport and are then scaled, so inside the app `dvh` is
   exactly as wrong as `vh` (Marina's ruling, EldenSpire#15). `height: 100%`
   computes 1361.29px = 844/0.62, which is correct, which is why base.css was
   already right to use percent below <body> and still is.
   <html> is the one element the zoom does not touch, so this is the one place a
   viewport unit is evaluated in the room it means. `100%` here resolves against
   the initial containing block, which on a phone tracks the LARGE viewport —
   the tall one you get when the address bar is hidden — so the bottom of the
   board sits under the bar whenever the bar is up. `100dvh` tracks the current
   one.
   UNVERIFIED, and I want that loud: headless Chromium has no moving address
   bar, dvh/svh/lvh all measure identically here, and this harness therefore
   cannot show this line doing anything at all. It is the one change on this
   branch with no measurement behind it. On a desktop it is a no-op (measured:
   1200x730 identical either way), which is why it is safe to leave in and
   dishonest to call it verified. */

/* UI size: the whole app is zoomed by --ui-zoom (Settings → UI size / Auto, set
   in main.js). Sizing uses PERCENT heights (not vh) everywhere below `body` so
   they resolve against the zoomed box and stay exactly viewport-sized — scaling
   up never overflows, scaling down still fills. (vh ignores zoom, which is what
   used to overflow.) */
body {
  background: radial-gradient(ellipse 60% 40% at 70% 10%, rgba(201, 162, 39, 0.06), transparent),
    linear-gradient(#16110c, var(--bg));
  color: var(--parchment);
  font-family: var(--font-body);
  font-size: 1.4rem;
  overflow: hidden;
  user-select: none;
  zoom: var(--ui-zoom, 1);
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
}

/* EldenSpire#23/#24 — the narrow layout is selected by `data-layout` on <html>,
   written by main.js's resolveLayout() in the same call that chooses --ui-zoom.
   The stylesheets measure nothing.

   The threshold is evaluated in the unzoomed viewport room. It intentionally
   remains independent of the height-aware --ui-zoom so browser chrome and the
   on-screen keyboard cannot flip the composition while a player is reading it.

   The answer turned out not to be a container query either. Asking the question
   in CSS at all made two deciders out of one decision — the zoom judging
   innerWidth/innerHeight against 430x780, the stylesheet judging the container's
   local width against 520 — and on a tablet they disagreed and the fight became
   unadvanceable (#24, 834x1194: zoom picks narrow at 1.53, layout stays wide at
   545 local px, END TURN 0/45 where dev is 45/45). An attribute has no room
   problem because it carries no length, and it cannot disagree with the zoom
   because the same function writes both.

   Removing it also retires `container-type: inline-size` and with it the WebKit
   unknown Sunna bounded on this branch — whether a query container becomes a
   containing block for fixed descendants. Nothing here declares one now. */
#app { height: 100%; display: flex; flex-direction: column; }

/* THE THREE EMPHASES, AND THE ONE THAT WAS MISSING.
   Measured with the corner census above: the tree had `button` (gold outline),
   `.subtle` (quiet outline) and `.danger` (red outline) — three ways to say
   "not the main thing" and NO way to say "this one". So a modal footer said it
   by accident instead: Load Game leaves BACK and CONTINUE the same size and
   weight and asks the border colour to carry the difference, and the in-run
   Settings footer paints Save and Quit in DANGER RED for an act that saves.
   `.primary` is the missing word. Red is now spent only on loss.

   ONE PER SURFACE is the rule this enables and does not enforce: nothing here
   can count the buttons in a footer. What it can do is make the emphasis a
   NAME a reviewer can see in the markup rather than a set of overrides they
   have to compare pixel by pixel. */
button.primary {
  background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--gold) 22%, var(--panel));
  border-color: var(--gold);
  color: var(--parchment);
}
button.primary:hover { background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--gold) 32%, var(--panel)); }
button.primary:disabled { background: var(--panel); border-color: var(--line); color: var(--muted); }

/* THE FOCUS RING, ONCE, IN THE HOUSE COLOUR.
   There was no app-wide rule, so anything without its own `:focus-visible`
   wore CHROME'S DEFAULT — a thick white double outline on a gold-on-brown
   panel. It is not hypothetical: settings.js:1591 focuses `.set-tab.on` on
   open, so opening Settings on a phone PAINTS it every time, and the census
   caught it on the 390x844 capture.

   `:where()` on purpose — specificity ZERO, so a component that must move the
   ring INWARD (a control inside a card, a tab) can set its own offset without
   out-ranking anything. The ink is never restated: `--focus-ring` (kit.css)
   is the one token, and the pad's cursor (`.gp-focus`, ui.css) wears the same
   ring. Since 2026-09-11 this is not a floor under fourteen rings — it IS the
   ring; the per-component box-shadow halos, 3px outlines and pale inks went. */
:where(a, button, input, select, summary, textarea, [role='button'], [tabindex]:not([tabindex='-1'])):focus-visible {
  outline: var(--focus-ring);
  outline-offset: var(--focus-ring-offset);
}

/* ---------- screen transitions (every mount fades in) ---------- */
#app > * { animation: screenIn 240ms ease-out; }
@keyframes screenIn {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(8px); }
  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}

/* Accessibility: honor reduced-motion for ALL animation (GDD §6).
   TRANSITIONS ARE OFF, NOT SHORT. The usual snippet sets
   `transition-duration: 0.01ms` on `*`, and that is a transition on EVERY
   property — `transition-property` defaults to `all`, so a style write is
   followed by a one-frame transition from the old value, and a synchronous
   read straight after the write still sees the old value. The map camera
   does exactly that (mapboard.js `sizeSvg` sets the SVG's height, then reads
   the scroller's scrollHeight to clamp its landing): under reduced motion it
   read 1136 px against a 2515 px canvas and clamped the entrance frame 1120
   px short of the door, at every width, only for players with the setting
   on (measured 2026-09-11; without the setting the same code lands). Nothing
   in the app waits on `transitionend`, so `none` is the honest value. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition: none !important;
  }
}

/* Manual override from Settings — applies regardless of the OS preference. */
.reduced-motion, .reduced-motion *, .reduced-motion *::before, .reduced-motion *::after {
  animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
  transition: none !important;
}

/* /styles/kit.css */
/* styles/kit.css — THE COMPONENT KIT, in the game.
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Every player-facing surface is composed from the pieces in this file and
   nothing else. The vocabulary is the kit artifact's (§03 sub-components,
   §04 assemblies, §05 bodies, §07 menus, §08 tooltips, §10 cards), under the
   same names, so a rule read on the kit page is the rule that runs here.

   THE SHELL'S OWN CLASSES ARE KIT ASSEMBLIES UNDER THE REPO'S NAMES. The kit
   page called them `.as-head`, `.as-foot`, `.as-iconbtn`, `.as-btnrow`; the
   game had already named the same assemblies `.modal-head`, `.modal-foot`,
   `.modal-iconbtn`/`.modal-close`, `.modal-btnrow`, and thirty tools read
   those names off the rendered page. So this file styles BOTH spellings with
   one rule each — the repo name is the hook, the kit name is the recipe — and
   nothing in styles/ui.css may draw shell chrome any more.

   SCALE. The kit page was authored at a 15px root; this game's root is 10px
   (html { font-size: 62.5% }). Every kit rem is ×1.5 here, once, at the
   declaration — never at a call site. Radii are px in both, unchanged.

   LAWS KEPT: no vw/vh (the body is zoomed by --ui-zoom); the tap floor is
   --tap-floor and the icon box is --iconbtn-size (base.css); rem for type
   and the boxes that hold it, px for geometry that must not scale with type;
   one home per fact.
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */

:root {
  /* the kit's own two page tokens the game lacked */
  --ink-dim: #b9ac91;
  --rule: #2a2419;
  --r-pill: 999px;
}

/* The name fills its line: an indent would overflow and disable centering.
   Shift half the trailing tracking instead, keeping the visible text centered. */
/* THE translateX COMPENSATION IS CORRECT. IT WAS REMOVED ONCE, IN ERROR, AND
   THIS PARAGRAPH IS THE RECORD SO IT IS NOT REMOVED AGAIN.

   `letter-spacing` adds its track AFTER the final glyph too, so a centred line
   has its INK sitting half a track LEFT of the box centre. The translateX puts
   it back. #910 deleted it, on a measurement that took a Range over the text
   as if that were the ink — but a Range INCLUDES the trailing advance, so it
   reported the uncompensated layout as perfectly centred. The number was real;
   it was measuring the wrong box, and it read 0px for a wordmark that was
   visibly off.

   Re-measured from PAINTED PIXELS — a screenshot scanned for the leftmost and
   rightmost lit column of the wordmark, which has no box model to be wrong
   about — as the ink's offset from the viewport centre, at three widths:

                          390      1200     2550
     with the transform   -1.5px   -1.5px   -2.5px
     without it           -3.0px   -3.5px   -5.5px

   The compensation roughly halves the error at every width. It is not a second
   correction for a solved problem; the browser does NOT discount the trailing
   advance when centring, and #910's claim that it does was wrong.

   startup-gate now subtracts the trailing advance before judging centring
   (A11.RESPONSIVE-SHAPE, and A11.CENTERING-DETECTOR is its self-test), so the
   gate and this rule finally agree. Before that fix the gate measured the raw
   advance box, which made the MISSING compensation look green — two errors
   cancelling — and that false green is what invited #910.

   `--ink-bias` IS THE SECOND, SEPARATE HALF OF THE SAME CORRECTION. Half a
   track centres the glyphs' ADVANCES; ink is narrower than advances by each
   end glyph's side bearing, and those do not cancel. In Cinzel 700 the
   leading A's left bearing is 0.008em and the trailing E's right bearing is
   0.045em (both read from a 1000px raster of each glyph), so the ink sits
   (0.045 - 0.008) / 2 = 0.0185em LEFT of its advances' centre. That is about
   1px at 1x, which is why it hid inside the tolerance — but `body { zoom }`
   is 1.7 at 2550x1305, and at Text XL (57.6px) it grew to 1.8px of the
   -2.67px startup-gate read there against its 2.5px ink budget. It is an em
   quantity, so it scales with the type and the zoom and needs no per-shape
   tuning. Inter (the readable-ui face) reads 0.0136em, within 0.3px at this
   size, so one token serves both. It is specific to the A…E lockup: a
   different name needs its own end-glyph bearings measured. */
.as-titlemenu .tm-name { --track: 0.08em; --ink-bias: 0.0185em; margin: 0; transform: translateX(calc(var(--track) / 2 + var(--ink-bias))); font: 700 5.4rem/1.25 var(--font-display); font-size: min(12cqi, 5.4rem); letter-spacing: var(--track); text-indent: 0; color: var(--parchment); white-space: nowrap; text-shadow: 0 2px 24px rgba(var(--accent-rgb), 0.28); }
.as-titlemenu .tm-sub { --track: 0.28em; margin: 0.75rem 0 0; font-size: 1.05rem; letter-spacing: var(--track); text-indent: var(--track); text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--muted); white-space: nowrap; }
.as-titlemenu ul { list-style: none; margin: 1.8rem 0; padding: 0; }
.as-titlemenu li + li { border-top: 1px solid var(--rule); }
.as-titlemenu .tm-entry {
  display: block; width: 100%; min-height: var(--tap-floor);
  padding: 1.05rem 0;
  background: transparent; border: 0; border-radius: 0;
  color: var(--parchment);
  font: 600 1.88rem/1 var(--font-display);
  --track: 0.1em;

   one used to swallow the tap that landed on it — measured at 390x844 on

/* ═══ THE CARD — one fixed box, fixed landmarks, one shared row budget ═════ */
/* `.card` is the hook every screen and tool reads; `.as-card` is the recipe.
   THE BOX IS FIXED — `height`, not a floor — and its total is spelled out from
   its landmarks so a landmark that changes moves the box with it. Below the
   band there is ONE budget of rows that tags and text share: one tag row
   leaves three lines of text, two leave two. Both full is the only case that
   truncates; selecting the face reveals its Information button for full text. */
:root {
  --card-w: 14rem;
  --card-name-h: 2.6rem;      /* FIXED. two lines' worth of room, one line of type */
  --card-art-h: 6rem;         /* FIXED. */
  --card-band-h: 1.7rem;      /* FIXED. */
  --card-row: 1.5rem;         /* one row of the shared budget */
  --card-body-rows: 4;
  --card-pad: 0.8rem;
  --card-gap: 0.4rem;
}
.card, .as-card {
  position: relative;
  box-sizing: border-box;
  width: var(--card-w);
  height: calc(var(--card-name-h) + var(--card-art-h) + var(--card-band-h) + var(--card-body-rows) * var(--card-row) + 3 * var(--card-gap) + 2 * var(--card-pad) + 1.2rem);
  padding: calc(var(--card-pad) + 1.2rem) var(--card-pad) var(--card-pad);
  display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: stretch; gap: var(--card-gap);
  background: var(--bg-raise);
  border: 1px solid var(--line-soft);
  border-radius: var(--r-3);
  color: var(--parchment);

  transition: transform 140ms, box-shadow 140ms, border-color 140ms;
}

/* SELECTION CHANGES COLOUR, NEVER FOOTPRINT — the same signal as an OptionCard. */

/* THE CHOSEN CARD WEARS ONE GREEN RING, AND NOTHING STANDS UNDER IT.
   Victory wrote this signal first (`.reward-selected`): the card you picked is
   ringed in green, on its own edge. Every other card picker now borrows the
   SAME ring — creation's kit, the stables' mounts — because a player who
   learns the signal at the spoils door should not have to learn a second one
   in the Armoury, and because a word printed under the art ("Selected") reads
   as a button you can press when it is really a state you are in.
   GOLD STAYS HOVER, FOCUS AND INSPECTION; GREEN IS THE CHOICE THAT STANDS.
   `.hand .card.selected` in combat is deliberately NOT this: an armed card is
   a momentary aim you can still cancel, not a commitment, and it keeps the
   gold lift combat.css gives it.
   Two arms because the two card families are drawn differently — a `.card`
   carries its own border, while an `.equipment-poker-card` is only the aspect
   box and the frame it draws is `.epc-frame`, whose inset bevel has to
   survive the ring (restated here, not dropped). */

/* THE TWO-ROW BUDGET IS MEASURED, NOT GUESSED IN CALC. This rule used to clamp
   the strip with `max-height: calc(2 * (1.5rem + 0.3rem))`, which is a guess at
   what a chip row costs — and the guess was low: a shipped `.ctag` measures
   17px against the 15px assumed, so even a correctly fitted two-row strip was
   clipped, and an over-long one lost whole rows with no ellipsis and no `+N`.
   fitCardFace() counts the rows on the real face and hides every chip past the
   second behind a `+N` chip, so the strip's natural height IS the budget.
   `overflow: hidden` stays only as the belt for the frame before the first fit. */

   THE SHAPE AND THE TRACKS ARE READ, NOT RESTATED. This rule used to write
   `aspect-ratio: 5 / 8` and `1fr 4fr 4fr 1fr` out longhand, which was the same
   pair of facts content/config/ui/components/card.json already declared — so
   editing the JSON moved the hand's layout arithmetic (HandLayout, via
   wireframeUi) and left the card's own face exactly as it was. Both halves now
   read one home; src/ui/models/CardSizeModel.js projects it onto :root and
   carries the note on which shape won. There is deliberately NO fallback here:
   an unprojected card is shapeless and loud, never quietly the wrong shape. */

/* ═══ QUICK SETTINGS — the utility rail, under the band on the right ══════ */
/* Fullscreen and music are the two controls that belong to the PAGE, not to
   whatever is on it. They ride a rail of their own: a vertical stack pinned to
   the right edge, immediately BELOW the band, over the surface's content.
   WHY NOT THE TOP-RIGHT CORNER, which is where they were for a day. Owner,
   2026-09-04: "move full screen and music … to anchored to top right corner
   and not block any text"; owner, 2026-09-05, with a screenshot of build
   0.4.0.1454: "I miss the old Hudson and music and full screen placement".
   The corner is inside the band, so keeping text out from under the pair meant
   every surface reserving a horizontal slice of its own top row — and the
   measurement is what settles it: at 360x800 the map's header reserved
   243 of 434 CSS px, 56% of the band, for a pair 106px wide, and the identity
   ellipsed to "FORSAKEN ·…" while the meters collapsed to 50px. Below the band
   the pair overlays content that was already yielding to it: `.field` in
   styles/combat.css pads its right edge for exactly this rail, and the map's
   route strip calls its own right margin "the HUD's utility gutter". Those two
   gutters were written for this placement and were never removed, so for a day
   the game reserved space in three places for two buttons.
   The band is the containing block (`.as-band { position: relative }`), so
   `top: 100%` follows the band's own height on every surface and at every text
   size without a number to keep in step. `--hud-quick-edge-gap` is authored
   (balance.ui.hudQuickSettings.edgeGapPx, planted on <html> by main.js) and
   divided by the zoom, so the gap is the same on glass at every UI size. */
/* THE RAIL'S FOOTPRINT, as one token the surfaces under it reserve. It is ONE
   IconButton wide, not two, because the rail is a COLUMN — the same value this
   token replaced when it was inlined in styles/combat.css. */
:root { --quick-corner: calc(var(--iconbtn-size) + (2 * var(--hud-quick-edge-gap, 4px) / var(--ui-zoom, 1))); }
.hud-quick-settings {
  position: absolute; z-index: 80;
  top: calc(100% + (var(--hud-quick-edge-gap, 4px) / var(--ui-zoom, 1)));
  right: calc(env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px) + (var(--hud-quick-edge-gap, 4px) / var(--ui-zoom, 1)));
  display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: flex-end; gap: 0.6rem;
  margin: 0; padding: 0;
}
/* The notice speaks to the LEFT of the rail rather than pushing it off the
   edge: the rail is a column now, so there is no room under it. */
.hud-quick-settings > .hud-quick-notice {
  position: absolute; top: 0; right: calc(var(--iconbtn-size) + 0.4rem);
  max-width: 22rem; text-align: right; white-space: normal;
}

/* NOTHING RESERVES A SLICE OF ITS OWN TOP ROW ANY MORE. The rail sits under the
   band, so the run header, the co-op banner and the co-op board top each get
   their full width back — that is the point of moving it, and re-adding a
   `padding-inline-end: var(--quick-corner)` to any of them would give the dead

   for this placement. */
/* A narrow map header cannot hold its whole line AND the corner, and `nowrap`
   made its actions overflow INTO the corner rather than yield. It wraps: the
   way out drops to its own line under the pair (kit law — a narrow shape is a

/* THE ROOMS WEAR THE MAP'S BAND (components/runHud.js): the merchant, the

.screen.room-screen { justify-content: flex-start; justify-content: safe flex-start; }

/* ═══ CARD SHELF — a row of resting cards, four across, whole ══════════════ */
/* WHAT THIS REPLACES. A shelf of cards you are browsing past was laid out five
   different ways: the merchant's armaments in `min(280px, 100%)` tiles (the
   FOCUS width, around a 152px GLANCE card), its relics and flasks in
   `flex: 1 1 26rem` OptionCards, a mount's deck list and the pile viewer in
   fixed 140px and 220px boxes. None of them said how many cards a row holds,
   so the answer was whatever the container happened to be — at 1328x744 the
   merchant's armament shelf held ONE, with the rest behind a scroll.

   THE RULE, ONCE. `maxColumns` cards across; each track as wide as the row
   allows, never below `--card-shelf-min` and never above a card's resting
   width; below that floor the row holds fewer rather than shaving them. The
   three numbers are authored at `content/config/ui/components/card.json ->
   sizing.shelf` and projected by CardSizeModel.js, whose `cardShelfColumnsAt`
   is this rule's arithmetic, asked from Node by tests/card-shelf.test.mjs.

   The floor is written `min(--card-shelf-min, --card-w-glance)` for the same
   reason the model clamps it: a card tuned (or a phone variant dropped) below
   the floor would otherwise be stretched to a floor wider than itself. */
.card-shelf {
  --card-shelf-track: max(
    min(var(--card-shelf-min, 120px), var(--card-w-glance, 152px)),
    calc((100% - (var(--card-shelf-cols, 4) - 1) * var(--card-shelf-gap, 12px)) / var(--card-shelf-cols, 4))
  );
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: flex-start;
  justify-content: center;
  gap: var(--card-shelf-gap, 12px);
  width: 100%;
  max-width: none;
}
/* NO GROW. A wrapping flex row lets the last row's stragglers spread into the
   slack beside them — measured on the merchant's five-card shelf at 1328x744:
   four cards at 145px and the fifth, alone on its row, at 155. One shelf, one
   card, two sizes. The track already fills the row, because
   components/cardShelf.js writes `--card-shelf-cols` from the count the shelf
   actually holds at its measured width, so there is nothing left for growth to
   do but break the agreement between the rows. */
.card-shelf > * {
  flex: 0 1 var(--card-shelf-track);
  min-width: 0;
  max-width: var(--card-w-glance, 152px);
  margin: 0;
}
/* A line of prose on a shelf is not a card: an empty shelf's "nothing for sale
   on this visit" would otherwise be squeezed into one 152px column. */
.card-shelf > :is(.as-status, p, h3, .shop-offer-avail) { flex-basis: 100%; max-width: none; }
/* NOR IS AN OFFER WITH NO CARD IN IT. The merchant's SELL shelf is mixed: an
   armament he will buy is a card, a relic or flask is an OptionCard with a
   name, a description and a price and no face at all. Capping THAT at a card's
   width ellipsised the name and stood the description in a 152px strip, so a
   tile that holds no card keeps the kit's own measure (`.class-pick`, kit
   above) and takes a row of its own. `.shop-collectible-offer` is the tile
   that DOES hold a face and is deliberately not exempt. */
.card-shelf > .shop-text-offer { flex: 1 1 26rem; max-width: 40rem; }

/* THE PLAYING CARD IS A FIXED BOX and `flex-shrink: 0`, so on a shelf it would
   have overflowed its track rather than fitting in it. `--card-w` is the box's
   one width input and the height is computed from its landmarks, not from the
   width — so a narrower card is the same card with its text clamped by the
   budget that already clamps it (`.ctext` line-clamp); Information opens the
   full text. */

   makes it small, and a transform on top of that only opens a gap. Hover and
   focus keep their lift. */

/* ASSIGN POINTS IS NARROWER THAN THE COLUMN THE RULE ABOVE WAS WRITTEN FOR.
   `white-space: normal` lets a summary read in full where there is room, which
   is right in Character Creation. Inside the Assign Points overlay there is not
   room: Intelligence's hint — the longest of the five — wraps to a second line,
   which takes its inner row from 29.41px to 43.44px and its card from the 44px
   tap floor the other four sit exactly on to 45.44px. Five cards, four at 44
   and one at 45.44, is no longer the one compact family this surface promises,
   and tools/uniform-stat-foldouts.mjs has been red on dev for it since #647.
   Measured in headless Chromium at 390x844.

   The compact face row already ellipsises by default (`.disc-face > .as-row
   .ls-hint`, above); this restores that default on the one surface too narrow
   to honour the wrap, which is what `.armoury-character-stats` does for the
   same content. Scoped to the overlay on purpose — Character Creation is wide
   enough to wrap without overflowing, and keeps the full sentence. */
.cc-stat-overlay .disc-faces > .disc-face .disc-summary {
  min-width: 0; white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
/* A FULL-WIDTH FACE IS A LINE OF ITS OWN, AND THE `.disc-faces >` IS LOAD-BEARING.
   Without it this reads `.disc-face.disc-pick` — two classes — and loses on
   specificity to `.as-options.flow > .as-option { flex: 1 1 auto }` three rules
   up, which is three. Measured at d51b46a, headless Chromium 1200x730: all four
   creation sections (CLASS / CHARACTER / STARTING EQUIP / SEED) computed
   `flex: 1 1 auto` and shared ONE line at top=77, so the one reveal — a
   `flex: 1 1 100%` row of the same wrap — could only ever land after the whole
   row. That is Constantine's "instead it just shows up at hte bottom", and it
   is the SAME defect MR-287 fixed in disclosure.js, re-opened by a stylesheet:
   the placement code was right and had nothing to place between. Scoped to the
   child combinator the count is three either way and the later rule — this one
   — wins, on flow hosts and column hosts alike. */
.disc-faces > .disc-face.disc-pick, .disc-faces > .disc-face.disc-armament, .disc-faces > .disc-face.disc-relic, .disc-faces > .disc-face.disc-item, .disc-faces > .disc-face.disc-power, .disc-faces > .disc-face.disc-stat, .disc-faces > .disc-face.disc-attribute, .disc-faces > .disc-face.disc-section { flex: 1 1 100%; }

/* ═══ METER — a resource read at a glance ══════════════════════════════════ */
/* Label · value · track. The TRACK's length is data (the surface writes its
   width inline: max ÷ reference, so a bigger pool is a longer bar), the fill is
   cur ÷ max. `.skinny` is the poise weight: no label, no value, a hairline
   track. `.inset` puts the value inside the track for the under-model strip,
   where there is no room beside it. Tones name the resource, never a screen. */
.as-meter { --meter-h: 10px; --meter-tone: var(--gold); position: relative; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.6rem; min-width: 0; width: 100%; container-type: inline-size; }
/* THE LADDER, MEASURED, NOT GUESSED (§02): a meter too narrow for its name
   drops the NAME and keeps the glyph and the value, because the value is the
   fact and the glyph is the identity. Only then does anything truncate. */
/* 9rem, AND rem RATHER THAN em, both measured. This rung was written `8em` and
   never fired once: font-relative units in a container query resolve against the
   container's OWN font-size, and these meters inherit 0.92rem = 9.2px, so 8em
   was 73.6 px — under every column the game actually draws (the arcane receipt's
   container is 130 px at 1200x730 and 80 px at 390x844, in the LOCAL px a
   container query compares, which the battlefield's scale then renders as 88 and
   68). The name stayed and clipped instead: "ARCANE …" at the desk, "A…" on the
   phone. 9rem = 90 px falls between those two columns, which is the cut this
   ladder is about — wide enough for HP/MP/SP wherever they are drawn (120 px at
   320 px of viewport), too narrow for a word. */
@container (max-width: 9rem) { .as-meter > .m-plate > .m-label { display: none; } }
.as-meter > .m-plate { flex: 0 0 auto; display: inline-flex; align-items: baseline; gap: 0.5rem; min-width: 0; white-space: nowrap; }
.as-meter .m-label { flex: 0 0 auto; white-space: nowrap; font: 600 1.05rem/1 var(--font-body); letter-spacing: 0.1em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--muted); }
.as-meter .m-value { flex: 0 0 auto; white-space: nowrap; font: 600 1.15rem/1 var(--font-body); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; color: var(--parchment); }
.as-meter > .m-well { flex: 1 1 auto; min-width: 0; display: flex; align-items: center; }
/* `stack` — the plate ABOVE the track, for a meter in a narrow column (under a
   combatant, in a list). THE NAME WRAPS RATHER THAN TRUNCATING, and the receipt
   grows downward to hold it. Measured on the arcane receipt at ?shot=combat,
   whose name is fifteen characters: "Arcane Exposure" wants 131 px and its
   column is 92 px at 1200x730 and 68 px at 390x844, so with the label on one
   nowrap line it read "ARCANE …" at the desk and "A…" on the phone — a label
   that has stopped being a word. The 8em rung above drops a name that does not
   fit a WIDE meter; in a stacked one there is a whole line to give it, and a
   two-line name costs the sprite nothing. The value never wraps and never
   truncates: it is the fact. */
.as-meter.stack { flex-direction: column; align-items: stretch; gap: 0.15rem; }
.as-meter.stack > .m-plate { display: flex; align-items: baseline; justify-content: space-between; gap: 0.6rem; }
.as-meter.stack .m-label { flex: 0 1 auto; min-width: 0; overflow: visible; text-overflow: clip; white-space: normal; overflow-wrap: normal; line-height: 1.2; }
/* The rung above is also what stops this wrap from becoming a letter-per-line
   column: at 390x844 the plate leaves the name about 20 px, and `anywhere`
   spelled ARCANE EXPOSURE downwards. `overflow-wrap: normal` keeps the break at
   the space, and under 9rem there is no name to break — the glyph says which
   school it is. */
.as-meter.stack .m-value { flex: 0 0 auto; }
.as-meter .m-track { position: relative; flex: 0 0 auto; box-sizing: border-box; width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: var(--meter-h); min-width: 0; padding: 0; border: 0; background: var(--bg); box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--line); border-radius: var(--r-pill); overflow: hidden; }
.as-meter .m-fill { position: absolute; inset: 0 auto 0 0; background: var(--meter-tone); border-radius: inherit; }
.as-meter[data-tone="hp"] { --meter-tone: var(--res-hp, var(--blood)); }
.as-meter[data-tone="mp"], .as-meter[data-tone="mana"] { --meter-tone: #4f82d8; }
.as-meter[data-tone="sp"], .as-meter[data-tone="stamina"] { --meter-tone: #5f925d; }
.as-meter[data-tone="poise"] { --meter-tone: var(--gold); }
.as-meter[data-tone="arcane"] { --meter-tone: #8a6fd6; }
.as-meter[data-tone="danger"] { --meter-tone: var(--danger); }
/* The two climbs: character XP in gold, a skill track in the cooler steel
   so a glance separates "the level" from "a track". */
.as-meter[data-tone="xp"] { --meter-tone: var(--gold); }
.as-meter[data-tone="skill"] { --meter-tone: #7fa8c9; }
.as-meter.inset { --meter-h: 13px; }
.as-meter.inset .m-label { display: none; }
.as-meter.inset > .m-plate { position: absolute; inset: 0; display: grid; place-items: center; pointer-events: none; z-index: 1; }
.as-meter.inset .m-value { font-size: 0.95rem; letter-spacing: 0.04em; text-shadow: 0 1px 2px #000; }
.as-meter.skinny { --meter-h: 4px; }
.as-meter.skinny > .m-plate { display: none; }
.as-meter.pulse .m-fill { animation: pulse-gold 600ms infinite alternate; }
.reduced-motion .as-meter.pulse .m-fill { animation: none; }
/* A dashed rim says "this length is the floor, not the data". */
.as-meter .m-track[data-floored="1"] { box-shadow: none; border: 1px dashed var(--line-soft); }
/* A meter that is locked reads dimmed; a striped fill says a resistance holds. */
.as-meter.locked { opacity: 0.6; }
.as-meter.resisted .m-fill { background: repeating-linear-gradient(45deg, var(--meter-tone) 0 4px, transparent 4px 8px); }
/* A stack of meters, one under the other, tight. */
.as-meters { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.3rem; width: 100%; min-width: 0; }
.as-meters.tight { gap: 2px; }
/* Main Vitals use the shared screen-pixel token. Dividing by the page zoom
   makes the authored 3px separation land as 3px on glass at every UI scale;
   model strips retain the kit's tighter local stack. */
.resbars[data-surface="main"] { gap: calc(var(--hud-resource-row-gap-px) / var(--ui-zoom, 1)); }

/* ═══ SLOT — a square control that holds one thing: art, a count, a key ═══ */

/* ═══ BAND — a page-level chrome strip (the HUD, an action row, a zoom bar) ═ */
/* `.topbar` is the hook co-op's bar still writes; the kit name is the recipe. */
/* `position: relative` ON BOTH, because the utility rail hangs off the bottom
   of whichever one carries it (`top: 100%`, § QUICK SETTINGS). `.as-band`
   already had it for its grip; `.topbar` did not, and the co-op board's two
   headers (`screens/coop.js`) are bare `.topbar` with no `as-band` — so the
   rail would have escaped to the nearest positioned ancestor and hung a full
   screen height below the fold. hud-quick-compact's 18 surfaces are solo
   map/combat/title, so no gate would have said so. */
.as-band, .topbar { position: relative; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1.2rem; flex: 0 0 auto; min-width: 0; padding: 0.6rem 1.6rem; background: var(--bg-raise); border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line); }
.as-band.foot { border-bottom: 0; border-top: 1px solid var(--line); }
.as-band.stack { flex-direction: column; align-items: stretch; gap: 0.5rem; }
.as-band.quiet { background: transparent; border: 0; }
.as-band-row { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1.2rem; min-width: 0; width: 100%; }
/* THE METERS START LEVEL WITH THE CONTROLS BESIDE THEM. The resource row's
   height is set by its right-hand cluster — two rows of IconButtons, 112 CSS px
   at 360x800 — while the three meters are 41, so `align-items: center` left
   them straddling the gap between the ⚒ ☰ row and the flasks below, aligned to
   neither. Cross-axis only: the row's height is the cluster's either way, so
   this moves no other row and the map and combat HUDs stay the same height. */
.hud-resource-row { align-items: flex-end; }
.hud-resource-row > .hud-vitals-panel { align-self: flex-end; }

.as-band-row.split { justify-content: space-between; }
.as-band-row.end { justify-content: flex-end; }
.as-band-row.center { justify-content: center; }
/* Three tracks: identity, a centred receipt, the trail — the run header's shape. */
.as-band-row.thirds { display: grid; grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) auto minmax(0, 1fr); align-items: center; }
.as-band-row.thirds > :last-child { justify-self: end; }

/* ═══ BAND FOLD — ONE FACT LINE AND ONE METER LINE ════════════════════
   A HOST that gives the shared band less room than its two full-width rows
   need FOLDS it, and the fold is one rule set here, not one per host. Two ask
   for it and they asked differently, which is the defect this block closes:
   the map's W4b header (§ MAP HEADER, `data-hud-layout="map-compact"`) carried
   these rules alone, and when W4c's dialogue band took the same fold
   (§ DIALOGUE, `data-hud-compact='true'`, 2026-09-17) it took the GRID and
   left the yielding behind — so at 430 wide the three fact tracks and the
   stacked meters overflowed their half-width columns and printed on top of
   each other. A fold that is copied is a fold that is copied wrong.

   WHAT YIELDS, in the text law's order. The row keeps its three tracks at
   every width, because the centred receipt is centred at every width and that
   is the whole point of the middle track. What gives is DETAIL: a chip may
   shrink, and the class name and the act's seat name ellipsize inside their
   own track rather than running over Cinders. Keys and numbers never do.
   The meters stop stacking and sit side by side on one line. */
.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
.dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud { --band-fold-gap: calc(8px / var(--ui-zoom, 1)); }
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .hud-info-row > .as-statstrip {
  min-width: 0; margin: 0; flex-wrap: nowrap;
}
/* The trail FILLS its track and packs right, rather than the kit's
   `justify-self: end` (above), which sizes it to its max-content and lets it
   run left over Cinders on a phone instead of yielding. */
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .hud-info-row .hud-run-meta {
  justify-self: stretch; justify-content: flex-end; gap: 0 var(--band-fold-gap);
}
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .hud-info-row .as-chip {
  display: flex; flex: 0 0 auto; min-width: 0; white-space: nowrap;
}
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .hud-info-row :is(.hud-class, .hud-act) { flex: 0 1 auto; }
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .hud-info-row .as-chip > .ck { flex: 0 0 auto; }
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .hud-info-row :is(.hud-class, .hud-act) > .cv {
  display: block; flex: 0 1 auto; min-width: 0; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap;
}
/* One meter line: HP, MP and SP side by side instead of stacked. */
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .resbars {
  display: grid; grid-auto-flow: column; grid-auto-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);
  column-gap: calc(10px / var(--ui-zoom, 1)); row-gap: 0;
}
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .resbars > .resline {
  min-width: 0; gap: calc(6px / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
}
:is(.as-band-fold, .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"],
    .dialogue-screen[data-hud-compact='true'] .shared-hud) .resbars .resunit { gap: calc(5px / var(--ui-zoom, 1)); }
/* ═══ BAND ON A PHONE — THE SAME BAND IN EVERY VIEW ══════════════════
   THE OWNER'S RULE (2026-09-18): "just vertically stacked vitality block,
   cinders, armament and menu button. should be uniform in every view. act and
   floor should show up in wide screen but on mobile, that's how it should be."

   So on a phone the band carries FOUR THINGS and nothing else: the three
   meters STACKED, the Cinders receipt, Armoury, Menu. The class name, the act
   and the floor are WIDE-SCREEN FACTS — they are not truncated on a phone,
   they are not there. A phone reads the same band on the map, in a room, in a
   fight and in a conversation, which is what "uniform in every view" means and
   what neither the fold nor the map header gave it before: the fold's one
   meter line and its ellipsized act chip are a WIDE answer to a narrow band,
   and they stop at this gate.

   THE GATE IS THE PUBLISHED ONE. `data-layout="narrow"` is written on <html>
   by main.js's applyUiScale from balance.ui.uiScale.narrowMax (520 visual px),
   by the same call that chose the zoom. This block re-measures nothing. */
:root[data-layout='narrow'] .shared-hud .hud-info-row > :is(.hud-identity, .hud-run-meta) { display: none; }
/* The receipt keeps the middle track of § BAND thirds, so it stays centred
   with its neighbours gone rather than sliding to an edge. */
:root[data-layout='narrow'] .shared-hud .hud-info-row > .hud-center { grid-column: 2; justify-self: center; }
/* STACKED, in every host. This outranks § BAND FOLD's one meter line on
   purpose: the fold is what a band does when it is too short for its rows, and
   a phone answers that by dropping the wide facts instead. */
:root[data-layout='narrow'] .shared-hud .resbars {
  display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: stretch; row-gap: calc(4px / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
}
:root[data-layout='narrow'] .shared-hud .resbars > .resline { min-width: 0; }
/* "JUST" IS FOUR THINGS, so the map's route receipt goes with the act chip it
   restates — the same act name, one line lower. A phone's band is the band,
   not the band plus this host's extra. The map still carries the route on
   every wider screen, where it sits beside the facts rather than under them. */
:root[data-layout='narrow'] .shared-hud .act-route-strip { display: none; }
/* The band takes the height its four things need. W4b's 10 vh and W4c's band
   are WIDE-SCREEN heights, and a height that holds one folded line cannot hold
   three meters — honoured as a floor here, never as a ceiling. */
:root[data-layout='narrow'] .shared-hud[data-hud-layout="map-compact"] {
  height: auto; min-height: calc(var(--map-header-height-px, 80) * 1px / var(--ui-zoom, 1));
}

/* On a phone the three tracks stay three — the centred receipt is centred at
   every width, which is the whole point of the middle track — and what yields
   is DETAIL: a trail keeps the first part of each compound fact and drops the
   rest (a build keeps its number, drops its source). */
@media (max-width: 640px) {
  .as-band-row.thirds { gap: 0.5rem; }
  /* TWO SELECTORS, NOT ONE, and the phone photograph is why. A trail carries two
     shapes of compound fact: the build stamp (number · source) and a progress
     Chip (key, then value / total). `> * > :nth-child(n+2)` hit both — right for
     the stamp, wrong for the chip, where the second child IS the value: at
     390x844 the header read "ACT" and "FLOOR" with no numbers at all, which is a
     label announcing nothing. So the head of each fact stays and only its tail
     goes: the stamp keeps BUILD and drops src, the chip keeps "1" and drops
     "/ 12". */
  .as-statstrip.trail > .build-stamp > :nth-child(n+2) { display: none; }
  /* `> *` and not `:nth-child(n+2)`: the value itself is a TEXT NODE inside
     `.cv` and the "/ total" is the only ELEMENT in there, so counting elements
     from the second would keep the tail it is here to drop. */
  .as-statstrip.trail > .as-chip > .cv > * { display: none; }
  /* THREE TRACKS AT EVERY WIDTH, again. From 2026-08 to 2026-09-05 the phone
     shape was two tracks with the trail dropped to its own row, because the
     corner had taken the trail's track and the over-wide trail spilled onto
     the centred receipt. Both of the things that made that necessary are gone:
     the trail is empty (the build stamp left the band) and so is the identity
     cluster (name, class and floor left it the same day). With nothing in the
     outer tracks, a two-track grid only did harm — its `auto` middle track sat
     at the right edge, so the Cinders receipt read right-aligned at 390 and
     320 wide (hudparity `cinders-centre`, twelve findings; Constantine:
     "cinder should be centered"). The wide rule above now holds here too. */
  /* ONE LINE FOR THE IDENTITY'S EYEBROW, so the run HUD is the SAME HEIGHT on
     every screen that draws it. The context line beneath it is already nowrap;
     the eyebrow was not, so it wrapped wherever its track was tightest — and
     the map's track is tighter than combat's, which made the map's HUD 19px
     taller than the same HUD one screen earlier (hud-quick-compact:
     "Map and Combat draw different HUDs"). A HUD that changes height as you
     walk through a door moves every control under it. It truncates instead,
     which is the step the text law names after the box has stopped yielding. */
  .hud-identity > .as-eyebrow { white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }
  /* PADDING YIELDS BEFORE THE ROW WRAPS, which is the first step of the text
     law and the second half of the same equal-height problem. `.hud-top` is
     content-sized, so the trail's track is as wide as the widest row beside it
     — 159px on the map, which carries no flask belt, against 247px in combat.
     At the kit's 1.35rem column gap the map's three facts wanted 168px, so the
     build stamp dropped to a second line and the map's HUD grew a row. The
     gap gives up 8.5px instead; all three facts keep their whole text and both
     screens draw the same HUD. */
  .as-statstrip.trail { gap: 0.75rem 0.5rem; }
}
/* A cluster is a group of IconButtons or Slots that share one gap. */

/* ═══ HOLD — the second beat on a control ══════════════════════════════════ */
/* `.beat-hold` is written by the machinery (components/holdconfirm.js) on any
   control the second-beat table arms; `--hold` is 0..1 per frame. The fill is a
   high-contrast light/dark stripe instead of an accent wash: accent-filled
   primary buttons already look lit, so another gold layer disappears on them.
   Alternating luminance stays legible on both primary and plain controls. It
   is a BACKGROUND (paints under a bare text node), never eased (an abort must
   read instantly), and it survives reduced-motion because it is state, not motion.
   `.hold-hint` is the word beside the label; it leaves an icon-sized control
   and leaves the control a focus cursor is on (a pad confirms in one press). */
.beat-hold, button.beat-hold, .as-btn.beat-hold,
button.beat-hold:hover, .as-btn.beat-hold:hover,
button.beat-hold:focus, .as-btn.beat-hold:focus,
button.beat-hold:active, .as-btn.beat-hold:active {
  background-image: repeating-linear-gradient(135deg,
    rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.52) 0 8px,
    rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.58) 8px 16px);
  background-repeat: no-repeat;
  background-size: calc(var(--hold, 0) * 100%) 100%;
  transition-property: border-color, color, transform;
}
.beat-hold[data-hold-feedback="delegated"], .beat-hold[data-hold-feedback="delegated"]:hover,
.beat-hold[data-hold-feedback="delegated"]:focus, .beat-hold[data-hold-feedback="delegated"]:active { background-image: none; }
.beat-hold[data-hold="holding"] { border-color: var(--gold); }
.hold-hint { margin-left: 0.6em; font-size: 0.75em; letter-spacing: 0.14em; color: var(--gold); opacity: 0.75; }
/* IN A ROW THE WORD FOLLOWS THE LABEL, NOT THE TRAIL. The trail takes the row's
   free space with `margin-left: auto`, so a hint appended after it (which is
   where the machinery appends it — it dresses the control, not the row) landed
   past the keycap and was clipped by the panel's padding box. Ordering it ahead
   of the trail puts it where it reads, beside the verb it qualifies. */
.as-row > .hold-hint { order: 0; flex: 0 0 auto; }
.as-row > .as-status, .as-row > .r-trail { order: 1; }
.gp-focus > .hold-hint, .as-slot .hold-hint, .flask-slot .hold-hint { display: none; }

/* ═══ A SEGMENTED CONTROL MAY WRAP RATHER THAN LOSE ITS TAIL ═══════════════ */
/* Measured at 390x844 in the run's Settings pane (☰ → Settings → Game): the Map
   zoom row's seven options are 342 px of content inside a 311 px pane, so the
   last option — 200 — fell outside the pane, and `.as-seg`'s own
   `overflow: hidden` cut it in half. A choice the player cannot see is a choice
   they do not have, and the pane's `overflow-x: auto` is not the answer either:
   nothing on the row says there is more of it to the right.
   So on a narrow shape the group wraps. It grows downward, where the pane
   already scrolls on purpose, and every option keeps its own tap box. The
   separator between two buttons is dropped when it wraps because a border-left
   on the first button of a new line is a hairline hanging off nothing; the
   group's own border still says where the control begins and ends. */
@media (max-width: 700px) {
  /* The trail has to be ALLOWED to be narrower than its contents first: it is
     `flex: 0 0 auto` on a nowrap row, so the group was handed its max-content
     295 px inside a 311 px pane and never wrapped at all (measured; wrapping
     `.as-seg` alone changed nothing). */
  .as-row > .r-trail, .as-option > .r-trail { flex: 0 1 auto; min-width: 0; flex-wrap: wrap; justify-content: flex-end; }
  .as-seg { flex-wrap: wrap; }
  .as-seg button + button { border-left: 0; }
  .as-seg button { border: 1px solid var(--line-soft); margin: -1px 0 0 -1px; }
}

/* CONTAINMENT, AND WHERE IT STOPS.
   `contain: layout paint` on the art wells below is free: they already declare
   `overflow: hidden`, so paint containment clips nothing that was not already
   clipped, and their only child is a statically positioned <img>, so layout
   containment steals no containing block from anyone. What it buys is that a
   sprite swapping frames inside one card cannot dirty the layout or the paint
   of the gallery around it — which on a phone scrolling forty cards is the
   difference between one invalidated box and forty.

   It stops at the well, and the stopping point is the load-bearing part.
   ui/cardEffectLayers.js mounts its planes absolutely, at percentage offsets
   under `translate(-50%,-50%)`, DELIBERATELY extending past the face they
   decorate — the overhang is the effect. Today they mount on `.card-flight`
   (combat.js), a fixed-position wrapper on <body> that holds a card ghost, so
   the wells below never host one and this containment is provably inert.
   That is a fact about the current call site, not a property of the selector:
   lifting `contain` to `.card` — or mounting a layer inside `.art` — would
   clip every hit spark to a border, and would look harmless in review because
   nothing else in this file mentions the layers. Hence this paragraph. */
.armoury-card-gallery .art { min-height: calc(55px / var(--ui-zoom, 1)); overflow: hidden; contain: layout paint; }

/* One fixed grid track size prevents the last row from stretching its cards. */
/* THE PICKER IS STYLED BY ITS STATE, NOT BY WHAT IS INSIDE IT (2026-09-18).
   `.cc-card-selectors` used to be matched here by `:has(.poker-equipment-choice)`
   — a content sniff. `:has()` takes the specificity of its most specific
   argument, so that selector (0,3,0) and the section's own (0,4,0) both
   outranked `.as-options[data-view="grid"]` (0,2,0) — which, before this
   change, was the only rule in the kit that `data-view` drove at all (the
   picker's own two branches below are the rules this change adds).
   The screen wrote the player's choice onto the container
   (customize.js) and the stylesheet then ignored it, so List and Grid rendered
   the same grid — and there was no `[data-view="list"]` rule anywhere, so even
   at equal specificity List had nothing to apply. The toggle had one authored
   state, not two.
   The picker arm therefore reads the container's own `data-view` now. The
   armoury and shop shelves have no toggle and keep the sniff; consolidating
   those onto one mechanism belongs with the card-size work, not here. */
/* THE MERCHANT'S SHELVES LEFT THIS RULE, 2026-09-20. `#shop-armaments`,
   `#shop-relics` and `#shop-flasks` were `auto-fill` tracks of up to 280px —
   the FOCUS width, for cards drawn at the 152px resting width — so the offers
   column fitted two tracks at best and one below 360px, with the rest behind a
   scroll. They are `.card-shelf` now, which is the one place that answers how
   many resting cards a row holds. The armoury's faces and the creation
   picker's grid keep the rule: their items are not resting cards. */

.cc-card-selectors[data-view="grid"] {

.armoury .disc-reveal:has(.poker-inventory-detail) { grid-column:1 / -1; }
